newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia seen pushing for Westward integration.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia seen pushing for Westward integration.

text.p: Slovenia's new government, voted in on Thursday after months of political stalemate, will continue pushing for entry to the European Union and NATO and for improved economic performance, analysts said on Friday.

Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek of the centre-left Liberal Democrats won parliament's approval for his cabinet more than three months after November elections which split the vote evenly between leftwing and rightwing parties.

Drnovsek, who failed in his first attempt last month to win parliamentary approval for his government, succeeded after forming a coalition with the conservative People's Party and the pensioner's party Desus, securing him 49 seats in the 90-seat chamber.
"In principle this coalition should be able to achieve a lot, but only if they are willing to show a great deal of readiness for compromise," political analyst Miha Kovac told Reuters.

Reforming the country's ailing pension system and reducing inflation from its current 8.5 percent would be the main domestic goals, while joining the EU and NATO would remain the key strategic tasks of foreign policy, analysts said.
Slovenia, which gained independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, is seen as well placed to win NATO membership in the first round of the alliance's expansion, possibly before the end of this year.
"The government's efforts towards joining Euro-Atlantic associations are most likely to continue, because there is no alternative for Slovenia," Kovac said.
Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats and the conservatives both hold nine posts in the new cabinet, while Desus got one.
The Liberal Democrats take the posts of foreign minister, finance minister and interior minister, while the People's Party will get the defence, justice and agriculture portfolios.

Zoran Thaler will be the new foreign minister. He held the same post for over a year until May 1996 when he was ousted over accusations that he had blocked Slovenia's assocciation agreement with the EU, which was finally signed in June 1996.

Marjan Podobnik, head of the People's Party, was named deputy prime minister. His party, which had opposed Drnovsek's first cabinet-line up in January, had previously pushed for Podobnik to be the new head of government.

"The effectiveness of the new government will depend on the quality of the cooperation between the Liberal Democrats and the People's Party," said Peter Krassnig, an analyst at Nova Ljubljanska Banka.
Market observers said the government would face the important challenges of overhauling the country's mergers and cross-border financial transaction legislation.
"The Bank of Slovenia and the Ministry of Finance have a dominant influence on the capital market and there will be no changes there," Mateja Gubanec, a trader at A bank said.
"But the approval of the government is positive because it enables the state to function normally and gives foreign investors a partner to talk to," Gubanec said.
